A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same LEXAM benchmark derived from 340 law exams. Their complete main texts, tables, figures, and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching relocated material.

before.justification: v3 reports original evaluations of 19 LLMs, MCQ perturbation experiments, and a three-expert study of 50 question–answer pairs.

after.justification: v4 reports original evaluations of 26 LLMs, ensemble-judge experiments, and additional quantitative and qualitative analyses using expert annotations.

M1.justification: v3 uses GPT-4o alone to grade open questions. v4 Section 3.1 replaces this central evaluation component with the minimum score from GPT-4o, DeepSeek-V3, and Qwen3-32B. This changes the judging procedure; the answer-generation and judging prompts in Appendix E remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same English/German exam coverage: 2,841 open questions, 1,660 standard MCQs, and 385 auxiliary MCQs with 4/8/16/32 choices. Dataset statistics and represented jurisdictions remain unchanged. The additional jurisdictions discussed in v4 Appendix J are future collection plans.

E2.justification: The main comparison expands from 19 to 26 models, adding GPT-5, GPT-5-mini, GPT-5-nano, GPT-4.1-mini, GPT-4.1-nano, Qwen3-32B, and Qwen3-235B. Table 11 adds Claude-4-Sonnet, DeepSeek-R1, and Qwen3-32B as individual judges, plus four ensemble configurations. Gemini-2.5-Pro is retained, despite v3's inconsistent 'Gemini-Flash' wording.

E3.justification: The primary open-question scoring protocol changes from a single GPT-4o assessment to minimum-score ensemble grading, making the revised headline scores a different evaluation condition. v4 also introduces comparisons of judge combinations and language-stratified validation on the existing 50 annotated items. Dataset splits, answer-generation prompts, and MCQ perturbation settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v4 Appendices G.4–G.6 compare individual and ensemble judges and examine self/family bias; Appendices H and I add language-consistency tests and extend failure-mode analysis. Conversely, the open-question year, question-length, and answer-length panels in v3 Figure 8 disappear from v4 Figure 9, although their discussion remains. The existing MCQ perturbation analyses are retained.

E5.justification: v4 adds language-specific correlation p-values and language-effect regression p-values and R² in Tables 14–15. It removes v3's 'Judge S.E.' reporting based on three GPT-4o samples, including the sampling-temperature description. Bootstrap standard errors and the existing Alt-test statistical framework remain; no increase in repeated runs is established.

E6.justification: v4 adds extensive ensemble and individual-judge scores. For example, Gemini-2.5-Pro receives 67.40 under the ensemble, while its earlier GPT-4o-judged mean of 82.2 is retained as 82.23 in Table 13; this is a scoring-condition difference, not a model performance loss. Newly evaluated GPT-5 leads with 70.20 on open questions and 62.65% MCQ accuracy. Existing MCQ and perturbation accuracies are retained apart from precision.

T1.justification: The Alt-test's leave-one-out setup, difference-vector formulation, tolerance parameters, and multiple-testing correction are retained. v4 adds empirical analyses and an ensemble procedure, but no new theorem, proof, substantive derivation, or formal mathematical assumption.

C1.justification: The benchmark's scope, difficulty claims, and contribution of scalable expert-aligned legal-reasoning evaluation remain. The abstract and introduction now explicitly present designing and deploying an ensemble judge as part of the contribution, refining the earlier single-judge evaluation claim.

C2.justification: v4 adds substantive explanations concerning judge self/family bias, minimum-score aggregation, accessibility, cross-language consistency, judge leniency, and disagreement on borderline cases. Appendix J retains the earlier language-coverage and outdated-law limitations while adding a rationale for prioritizing jurisdictional depth. The new Ethics Statement also explicitly limits intended use to research and education.

D1.justification: v4 adds direct code/data links and an explicit release and reproducibility statement. Appendix G newly documents annotation-sample composition, supervisory involvement, and approximately 10 hours of work per expert, replacing the earlier 6–8-hour description. These are documentation changes; most prompts, inference settings, hardware, endpoints, and cost descriptions remain unchanged.

R1.justification: v4 adds Panickssery et al. (2024) and Spiliopoulou et al. (2025) to motivate judge-bias handling, alongside Fan et al. (2025) and new model references. Several earlier dataset references, including COLIEE and JEC-QA sources, disappear although the comparison table retains those datasets. The central positioning against existing legal benchmarks remains unchanged.

P1.justification: Related Work moves from Section 2 to Section 6, after the experimental and expert evaluations. The main-text Limitations section becomes Appendix J's future-collection discussion, and Ethics and Reproducibility statements are added. The introduction and evaluation narrative are rewritten, Appendix G is reorganized, and citations switch from numbered to author–year style.

P2.justification: v4 combines existing open-question and MCQ examples into a new side-by-side Figure 2, redraws several performance plots, and removes three panels from the supplementary open-question figure. The main results table changes its columns and expands its rows; Table 11 is enlarged, and Tables 13–15 are added. Existing dataset and MCQ perturbation figures are largely retained and relocated.

improvement.justification: The expanded judge comparisons, Table 13's disclosure of grader-dependent scores, and language-consistency checks make v4's evaluation more auditable than v3's primarily GPT-4o-based presentation. These gains are tempered by validation on the same 50 items, removal of repeated-judge variability reporting and three supporting plots, and an overbroad claim about the fully open-model ensemble: Table 11 shows it passes only with the replacement bonus. The net improvement is useful but limited.
